summary: Robert Childan opens his American Artistic Handcrafts shop in San Francisco on a Friday morning, anxiously awaiting a shipment of valuable items from the Rocky Mountain States. Japanese Trade Official Nobusuke Tagomi calls demanding the Civil War recruiting poster he commissioned, pressuring Childan with barely concealed insult. Later, an attractive Japanese couple (the Kasouras) enters the shop, warming Childan's heart with their understanding and appreciation of his rare American artifacts. Despite his fantasies about the young woman Betty, Childan focuses on his 2 PM appointment with Tagomi. Meanwhile, Frank Frink lies in bed in his Hayes Street room, haunted by the knowledge that he has been fired from the factory after speaking inappropriately to his boss Mr. Wyndam-Matson. As a Jew in the Japanese Pacific States, Frank faces dire consequences if he's blacklisted. He consults the I Ching with the question 'How should I approach Wyndam-Matson to come to decent terms with him?' and receives Hexagram Fifteen (Modesty), a favorable sign. When he asks 'Will I ever see Juliana again?' (his ex-wife), he receives Hexagram Forty-four (Coming to Meet), suggesting she is wrong for him. Tagomi, in his twentieth-floor office overlooking San Francisco Bay, consults the I Ching about his meeting with Childan and receives an ominous hexagram about imbalance. He suspects that his incoming guest, Mr. Baynes, may be a spy disguised as a Swedish plastics businessman.

themes.name: The nature of power and humiliation
The role of fate and chance
The disjunction between appearance and reality
Class and racial hierarchies in the occupied world

philosophical_concepts.name: The I Ching as guide to action

key_events: Tagomi's impatient phone call to Childan
The Kasouras' visit to the shop
Frank's I Ching consultation about his marriage
Tagomi's suspicion about Mr. Baynes' true purpose
narrative_observations: PKD establishes the alternate history world through small details and the interactions of three main characters. The I Ching serves as both a plot device and philosophical anchor, suggesting that reality is guided by deeper cosmic principles. PKD uses interior monologue to reveal each character's anxieties about status, authenticity, and survival in a world of Japanese and German dominance.
